claims.assertion: The GPS track shows one off-route segment 21:47–21:50 in which 1.76 km was driven where the optimal route covers 0.03 km, adding 1.73 km and straying up to 979 m from the optimal route; this is an unexempted detour under RD-1.

The rider's consent at 21:44 was to a stop ('pull in at the petrol station just ahead for one minute'), and the detour segment began at 21:47, so the agreed stop did not authorise this route change; the driver's own statement admits he treated the stop as licence for 'a small change of route'.

The driver cannot invoke a justified-reroute exemption: no traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window, and the only speed records on the optimal route were band 4 (30–39 km/h) and band 5 (40–49 km/h), neither of which is band 1 or 2 severe congestion; weather was fair.

This is a RydeTAXI metered trip, so the extra 1.73 km of unexempted detour enters the fare; the meter rate implied by the bill is $1.41/km ($27.23 ÷ 19.3 km), giving a refund of 1.73 × $1.41 = $2.44 (rounded to the cent).

The billed excess of 2.1 km at $1.41/km ($2.90) exceeds the sum of detour segments (1.73 km); the residual of about 0.37 km is map-matching noise exceeding the stated 0.25 km tolerance, but I claim only the segment-based $2.44 identified by the GPS facts.
The driver's 90-day record shows 2 disputes, 2 upheld, with route disputes at 0, so RD-6's 'repeated route dispute' condition is not met and I do not seek a flag_account on that basis.

weaknesses: The rider did agree in chat at 21:44 to the driver's petrol-station request (F7, F8), so the driver will argue the detour falls inside RD-3/RD-5 consent; I rebut it on timing and scope (the segment started 21:47, F3) and on the fact that the agreed 'just ahead' stop was never made, but the consent message is real and the judge will weigh it.
The driver's own statement (F9) frames the change as 'a small change of route' following the agreed stop, which could be read as the rider having accepted a reroute rather than merely a stop.

The traffic record does show the optimal route was only flowing at 30–49 km/h (F10, F11) and the trip ran 5.6 min over estimate (F2), which the driver may use as a soft 'reasonable cause' argument even though RD-4 requires a band 1/2 or an incident (F12), which is absent.

The claimed amount is small ($2.44) against a $40.18 metered bill (F6), and the billed excess ($2.90, F4) exceeds my segment-based figure, so the judge may cap recovery at the smaller of the two rather than the larger.
The rider's own profile shows a clean 0-dispute history (F14), which supports credibility but does not establish the route facts; the case still stands or falls on F3.

[F3 F7 F8] [RD-5 RD-3(a)]
D2: The rider's consent was given before the driver left the optimal route, satisfying the 'mutual agreement before you go' test in RD-5, so the 1.73 km added between 21:47 and 21:50 is exempt and draws no refund. [F3 F7 F8] [RD-5]
D3: The only remaining unexplained distance is the 2.10 km - 1.73 km = 0.37 km residual (F1 vs F3), which is a small route/GPS matching residual rather than a second detour segment, as RD-2 contemplates for the difference between fare-excess and the sum of segments. [F1 F3] [RD-2 RD-1]
D4: No waiver under RD-4 is needed because the off-route segment is already exempt under RD-5; the recorded traffic was merely moderate (band 4 on SLE, band 5 on TPE, F10, F11) with no incident at all near the route (F12), so congestion is not the driver's justification and is not claimed as one. [F10 F11 F12] [RD-4 RD-5]
D5: The $2.90 excess-distance component in F4 corresponds to the same 2.1 km already accounted for by the consented stop plus the 0.37 km residual, so the contestable metered overcharge on any strict reading is at most 0.37 km × $1.41/km ≈ $0.52, not the full excess. [F1 F3 F4] [RD-2]
D6 (VOID): Waiting was charged at $0.00 (F6), so no stop-duration fee was imposed on the rider for the petrol stop and RD-3(c) is not in issue. [F6] [RD-3(c)]
D7 (VOID): The driver's request was to 'pull in ... for one minute' for petrol (F7), which is a stop request rather than a long loop, and the app-recorded deviation lasted 3 minutes (F3), corroborating that the driver implemented the stop the rider agreed to. [F3 F7 F8] [RD-3(a) RD-5]
Weaknesses: The rider's own words in the complaint ('he never stopped for petrol anyway') are not contradicted by any system record on fuel purchase - there is no receipt fact - so the judge may find the driver took a 1.73 km/3 min excursion (F3) under the guise of a stop he did not actually make, which would push the segment outside the RD-5 consent. | The off-route segment went up to 979 m off the optimal route (F3); the driver's own statement (F9) says he thought 'a small change of route was fine', and a judge may read the rider's 'Sure, no problem' (F8) as consent to a stop only, not to a 1.73 km routing change, per the RD-3(b)/RD-5 narrow reading of consent scope. | The excess distance is real and metered: 19.3 km actual vs 17.3 km optimal, +12% (F1), billed as $2.90 (F4) on a RydeTAXI meter where detour km enter the fare directly (RD-2), so a strict judge could award the full $2.90 rather than the $0.52 residual. | The driver's profile shows 2 prior upheld disputes in 90 days (F15), which the rider can invoke for a flag_account request under RD-6 if any deviation is found unexempted.
Asks: no_action

events.body:
RIDER: We've reviewed your route dispute and you're getting $2.44 back.

The trip included a stretch of about 1.73 km where the driver went off the best route, straying well away from it, and nothing excused that detour.

We'll send the $2.44 as a Ryde voucher to your account. That's the full amount for the extra distance.

Your account stays in good standing — no flags or restrictions were added.

DRIVER: We've reviewed the route dispute on this trip and it was upheld in part.

One section of the trip — roughly 1.73 km — went off the best route and strayed far from it, and nothing excused that detour.

The rider will receive $2.44 as a Ryde voucher for that extra distance. This comes from Ryde, not from your earnings, and no other action is being taken on your account.

Your account shows no route disputes upheld in the last 90 days, so nothing changes for you. Keep to the suggested route where you can.

Had the driver carried a prior upheld route dispute in the last 90 days, RD-6 would add an account flag.

claims.assertion: The GPS track shows one off-route segment 21:47–21:50 in which 1.76 km was driven where the optimal route covers 0.03 km, adding 1.73 km and straying up to 979 m from the optimal route; this is an unexempted detour under RD-1.

The rider's consent at 21:44 was to a stop ('pull in at the petrol station just ahead for one minute'), and the detour segment began at 21:47, so the agreed stop did not authorise this route change; the driver's own statement admits he treated the stop as licence for 'a small change of route'.

The driver cannot invoke a justified-reroute exemption: no traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window, and the only speed records on the optimal route were band 4 (30–39 km/h) and band 5 (40–49 km/h), neither of which is band 1 or 2 severe congestion; weather was fair.

This is a RydeTAXI metered trip, so the extra 1.73 km of unexempted detour enters the fare; the meter rate implied by the bill is $1.41/km ($27.23 ÷ 19.3 km), giving a refund of 1.73 × $1.41 = $2.44 (rounded to the cent).

The billed excess of 2.1 km at $1.41/km ($2.90) exceeds the sum of detour segments (1.73 km); the residual of about 0.37 km is map-matching noise exceeding the stated 0.25 km tolerance, but I claim only the segment-based $2.44 identified by the GPS facts.
The driver's 90-day record shows 2 disputes, 2 upheld, with route disputes at 0, so RD-6's 'repeated route dispute' condition is not met and I do not seek a flag_account on that basis.

weaknesses: The rider did agree in chat at 21:44 to the driver's petrol-station request (F7, F8), so the driver will argue the detour falls inside RD-3/RD-5 consent; I rebut it on timing and scope (the segment started 21:47, F3) and on the fact that the agreed 'just ahead' stop was never made, but the consent message is real and the judge will weigh it.
The driver's own statement (F9) frames the change as 'a small change of route' following the agreed stop, which could be read as the rider having accepted a reroute rather than merely a stop.

The traffic record does show the optimal route was only flowing at 30–49 km/h (F10, F11) and the trip ran 5.6 min over estimate (F2), which the driver may use as a soft 'reasonable cause' argument even though RD-4 requires a band 1/2 or an incident (F12), which is absent.

The claimed amount is small ($2.44) against a $40.18 metered bill (F6), and the billed excess ($2.90, F4) exceeds my segment-based figure, so the judge may cap recovery at the smaller of the two rather than the larger.
The rider's own profile shows a clean 0-dispute history (F14), which supports credibility but does not establish the route facts; the case still stands or falls on F3.

claims.assertion: The single off-route excursion in this trip is exactly the petrol stop the rider approved in advance: chat #1 at 21:43 asked permission for a petrol stop and the rider replied 'Sure, no problem' at 21:44 (F7, F8), which is four minutes before the off-route segment started at 21:47 (F3).
claims.void_reason: citation check: cites RD-3(a) — not a citable clause

claims.assertion: The rider's consent was given before the driver left the optimal route, satisfying the 'mutual agreement before you go' test in RD-5, so the 1.73 km added between 21:47 and 21:50 is exempt and draws no refund.

The only remaining unexplained distance is the 2.10 km - 1.73 km = 0.37 km residual (F1 vs F3), which is a small route/GPS matching residual rather than a second detour segment, as RD-2 contemplates for the difference between fare-excess and the sum of segments.

No waiver under RD-4 is needed because the off-route segment is already exempt under RD-5; the recorded traffic was merely moderate (band 4 on SLE, band 5 on TPE, F10, F11) with no incident at all near the route (F12), so congestion is not the driver's justification and is not claimed as one.

The $2.90 excess-distance component in F4 corresponds to the same 2.1 km already accounted for by the consented stop plus the 0.37 km residual, so the contestable metered overcharge on any strict reading is at most 0.37 km × $1.41/km ≈ $0.52, not the full excess.
Waiting was charged at $0.00 (F6), so no stop-duration fee was imposed on the rider for the petrol stop and RD-3(c) is not in issue.
claims.void_reason: citation check: cites RD-3(c) — not a citable clause

claims.assertion: The driver's request was to 'pull in ... for one minute' for petrol (F7), which is a stop request rather than a long loop, and the app-recorded deviation lasted 3 minutes (F3), corroborating that the driver implemented the stop the rider agreed to.
claims.void_reason: citation check: cites RD-3(a) — not a citable clause

weaknesses: The rider's own words in the complaint ('he never stopped for petrol anyway') are not contradicted by any system record on fuel purchase - there is no receipt fact - so the judge may find the driver took a 1.73 km/3 min excursion (F3) under the guise of a stop he did not actually make, which would push the segment outside the RD-5 consent.

The off-route segment went up to 979 m off the optimal route (F3); the driver's own statement (F9) says he thought 'a small change of route was fine', and a judge may read the rider's 'Sure, no problem' (F8) as consent to a stop only, not to a 1.73 km routing change, per the RD-3(b)/RD-5 narrow reading of consent scope.

The excess distance is real and metered: 19.3 km actual vs 17.3 km optimal, +12% (F1), billed as $2.90 (F4) on a RydeTAXI meter where detour km enter the fare directly (RD-2), so a strict judge could award the full $2.90 rather than the $0.52 residual.
The driver's profile shows 2 prior upheld disputes in 90 days (F15), which the rider can invoke for a flag_account request under RD-6 if any deviation is found unexempted.

points.response: Consent under RD-5 must cover the segment agreed to: the rider agreed only to 'pull in at the petrol station just ahead for one minute' (F7, F8), while the GPS shows the actual off-route segment ran 21:47-21:50 for 1.76 km against 0.03 km on the optimal route, reaching 979 m off route (F3) — a 3-minute, 1.7 km excursion is not 'one minute at a station just ahead', so the consent does not reach this segment under RD-5/RD-3.

I accept that the 0.37 km difference between the billed 2.1 km excess (F1, F4) and the 1.73 km segment sum (F3) is not itself a second off-route segment, which is why my claim is confined to the 1.73 km segment and not to the full 2.1 km excess.

The driver's D4 concedes there is no incident on the route and only band 4/band 5 speeds (F10, F11, F12, F13), so no RD-4 exemption exists; since the RD-5 consent does not reach the 1.73 km segment (F3, F7, F8), that segment remains unexempted under RD-1 and is refundable under RD-2.

D5 double-counts the consent: because the agreed stop is not exempt (F7, F8 vs F3), the whole 1.73 km segment sits inside the contestable excess, so the RD-2 measure is 1.73 km × $1.41/km = $2.44 at the $1.41/km rate the bill itself implies (F6: $27.23 ÷ 19.3 km); the driver's own §D3 admits at most $0.52 only by assuming away the very segment in dispute.

I withdraw the characterisation in C5 that the 0.37 km residual breaches a 0.25 km tolerance; the residual is immaterial to my claim and I keep only the $2.44 segment-based figure, consistent with my concession on D3.

There is indeed one off-route segment (F3), but RD-1 only makes a segment 'unexempted' after it survives RD-3/RD-4/RD-5 review, and this one is covered by the pre-departure consent recorded in the chat (F7, F8).

Timing defeats the scope objection on its own terms: the rider's 'Sure, no problem' is timestamped 21:44 (F8) while the off-route segment did not begin until 21:47 (F3), so consent came before the driver left the optimal route, which is the only chronological test RD-5 sets.

RD-3(b) does not apply because it governs only cases where the rider named no place and the driver unilaterally chose one without telling the rider; here the driver named the petrol station 'just ahead' in chat #1 and the rider accepted it (F7, F8), and F9 is the driver's lay paraphrase of that same agreed stop rather than proof of a separate reroute.
points.void_reason: citation check: cites RD-3(b) — not a citable clause

points.response: Conceded: no incident was recorded near the route (F12) and the optimal route ran only at band 4 (F10) and band 5 (F11) in fair weather (F13), so the driver does not rely on RD-4 and rests the exemption on RD-5 consent instead of congestion.

The $1.41/km rate is not disputed (F4, F6), but the 1.73 km it is applied to (F3) is the consented petrol stop, so RD-2 refunds nothing on that segment; on the rider's own segmentation only the 2.10 - 1.73 = 0.37 km residual (F1 vs F3) is monetisable, about $0.52, not $2.44.

The rider's own concession that the 0.37 km residual is map-matching noise exceeding tolerance (F1, F3, F4) confirms the billed 2.1 km and the tracked segment describe the same event, leaving no second hidden detour for the meter to have captured.

Agreed and irrelevant here: the driver's 90-day record shows 0 upheld route disputes (F15), so no flag_account is sought under RD-6 against either party, whose profiles (F14, F15) are not relied on for the route finding.

For the avoidance of doubt, if the panel reads the consent scope narrowly and monetises the residual, the driver accepts at most 0.37 km x $1.41/km, approximately $0.52, using the 2.1 km billed in F1, the 1.73 km segment in F3 and the $1.41/km rate in F4 - not $2.90 and not $2.44.
